records.text: The army set out, and they encamped south of Emmaus.
Judas said, “Gird yourselves and become men of strength. Be ready in the morning to fight these nations that have gathered against us to destroy us and our holy places.
It is better for us to die in battle than to look upon the evils suffered by our nation and the holy places.
While we stayed for several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man whose belt this is in this way and hand him over into Gentile hands.’”
When we heard these things, both we and the local people urged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
After these days we made our preparations and went up to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea also went with us, taking us to a certain Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.
But now you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.
Therefore, if someone knows the good he ought to do and does not do it, it is sin for him.
All who were at the rear fell by the sword. They pursued them as far as Gazera and the plains of Idumea, Azotus, and Jamnia; about three thousand of their men fell.
Judas and his force returned from pursuing them,
and he said to the people, “Do not covet the spoils, because a battle lies before us.
Gorgias and his force are in the mountain near us. Stand now against our enemies and fight them; afterward take the spoils freely.”
While Judas was finishing these words, a detachment appeared, looking out from the mountain.
Seeing these things, they became exceedingly afraid. When they also saw Judas’s army on the plain ready for battle,
they all fled into the land of foreigners.
Judas returned to plunder the camp, and they took much gold and silver, blue cloth, sea-purple cloth, and great wealth.
On their return they sang hymns and blessed Heaven: “For it is good, for His mercy is for ever.”
A great deliverance came to Israel that day.

The Lord said to Joshua, “Stretch out your hand with the javelin you hold toward the city, for I have delivered it into your hands. The ambush shall rise quickly from its place.” Joshua stretched out his hand, with the javelin, toward the city,
and the ambush rose quickly from its place. They came out when he stretched out his hand, went to the city, captured it, and hurried to burn it with fire.
The others came out of the city to meet them, and they were caught between the forces, some on this side and some on that. They struck them until no survivor or fugitive remained.
They captured the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua.

When the sons of Israel finished killing all Ai’s people in the plains and on the mountain, on the descent where they pursued them from it to the end, Joshua returned to Ai and struck it with the edge of the sword.
Judas and his brothers said, “Behold! Our enemies have been crushed. Let us go up to cleanse the holy places and dedicate them anew.”
The whole army gathered, and they went up to Mount Zion.
They saw the sanctuary desolate, the altar profaned, the gates burned down, plants growing in the courts as in a thicket or on one of the mountains, and the chambers demolished.
They tore their garments, lamented with a great lament, and put ashes on themselves.
They fell face down upon the ground, sounded the signal trumpets, and cried to Heaven.
Then Judas ordered men to fight those in the citadel until he had cleansed the holy places.
They cleansed the holy places and carried the stones of defilement to an unclean place.
They deliberated what to do with the altar of whole burnt offering, which had been profaned.
They considered it best to pull it down, so that it would not become a reproach to them because the nations had defiled it. They pulled down the altar
and placed the stones on the mountain of the house in a suitable place until a prophet should come to give an answer about them.
They took whole stones according to the law and built a new altar like the former one.
“And now this command is for you, priests.

If you do not listen and do not take it into your hearts to give glory to My name,” says the Lord Almighty, “I will send out the curse upon you, and I will curse your blessing, and I will curse it. I will scatter your blessing, and it will not be among you, because you do not take it into your hearts.
Look, I am setting apart the shoulder for you, and I will scatter the stomach on your faces, the stomach of your festivals, and I will take you to the same place.
You will recognize that I have sent out this command to you, so that My covenant might be with the Levites,” says the Lord Almighty.
“My covenant with him was of life and peace, and I gave it to him in fear, to fear Me and to shrink back before My name.
But you have turned aside from the way and weakened many through the law; you have corrupted the covenant of Levi,” says the Lord Almighty.
“And I have made you despised and neglected among all the nations, because you did not guard My ways but showed partiality in the law.”
He took those from Galilee and Arbattos, with their wives, children, and everything they had, and brought them into Judea with great gladness.
Judas Maccabeus and Jonathan his brother crossed the Jordan and travelled a three-day journey in the wilderness.
They met the Nabateans, who received them peacefully and recounted everything that had happened to their brothers in Gilead.
Many of them had been confined in Bosora, Bosor in Alema, Chaspho, Maked, and Carnaim—all these cities were strong and large.
Judas and his army suddenly turned their route toward Bosora through the wilderness. He seized the city, killed every male with the edge of the sword, took all their spoils, and burned it with fire.
He set out from there by night, and they travelled as far as the stronghold.
In the morning they raised their eyes and saw a great people beyond counting, carrying ladders and siege engines to seize the stronghold and attacking its defenders.
Judas saw that the battle had begun and that the city’s cry rose to heaven with trumpets and a loud shout.
He said to the men of the force, “Fight today for our brothers!”
He came out behind them in three divisions. They sounded the trumpets and cried out in prayer.
Timothy’s army recognized that it was Maccabeus and fled before him. He struck them a great blow, and about eight thousand of their men fell that day.

He spoke to King Artaxerxes, saying, “There is a nation scattered among the nations throughout your kingdom. Their laws are unlike those of all the nations; they disobey the king’s laws, and it is not advantageous for the king to let them be.
If it pleases the king, let him decree their destruction, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the king’s treasury.”
The king removed his ring and put it into Haman’s hand to seal the written measures against the Jews.
The king said to Haman, “Keep the silver; deal with the nation as you wish.”

The king’s scribes were summoned on the thirteenth of the first month. As Haman commanded, they wrote to the generals and rulers in every territory from India to Ethiopia, the hundred and twenty-seven territories, and to the rulers of the nations in their own language, by authority of King Artaxerxes.

This is the copy of the letter: “The great King Artaxerxes writes the following to the rulers of the hundred and twenty-seven territories from India to Ethiopia and to the district governors subject to them:

Having ruled many nations and gained control of the whole inhabited world, I have wished—not exalting myself through the boldness of authority, but always conducting myself with greater fairness and gentleness—to establish the lives of my subjects in perpetual calm, to provide a civilized kingdom open to travel to its furthest limits, and to renew the peace desired by all people.

When I asked my counselors how this might be brought to completion, Haman, who excels among us in sound judgment, has demonstrated unchanging goodwill and firm loyalty, and has received the second honor in the kingdom,

pointed out to us that among all the tribes throughout the inhabited world a certain hostile people is intermingled, opposed in its laws to every nation, continually disregarding the kings’ decrees so as not to accept the shared administration that we direct blamelessly.

We have therefore understood that this nation alone stands in continual opposition to every person, differing through its strange observance of laws, showing ill will toward our affairs, and accomplishing the worst evils so that the kingdom may not enjoy stability.

We have therefore commanded that all those indicated to you in the writings of Haman, who is appointed over our affairs and is our second father, be destroyed root and branch, with wives and children, by the swords of their enemies, without any pity or sparing, on the fourteenth of the twelfth month, Adar, of the present year,
so that those hostile both formerly and now may go down violently to Hades in a single day and thereafter leave our affairs stable and undisturbed for all time.”
The copies of the letters were posted in every territory, and all the nations were ordered to be ready for that day.
The matter was also hurried forward in Susa. The king and Haman were drinking heavily, while the city was troubled.
Judas gathered all Israel in Gilead, from small to great, with their wives, their children, and their belongings—a very great company—to go into the land of Judah.
They came as far as Ephron. It was a large, exceedingly strong city on the road, and there was no way to turn aside from it to the right or left, but only to pass through its midst.
The people of the city shut them out and blocked the gates with stones.
Judas sent to them with peaceful words, saying, “We will pass through your land to go to our land. No one will harm you; we will only pass through on foot.” But they would not open to him.
Judas ordered a proclamation through the company that each should encamp in the place where he was.
The men of the force encamped. He attacked the city all that day and all that night, and the city was given into his hand.
He destroyed every male with the edge of the sword, uprooted the city, took its spoils, and passed through the city over the slain.
They crossed the Jordan into the great plain opposite Beth-shan.
They went up to Mount Zion with gladness and joy and presented whole burnt offerings, because none of them had fallen before they returned in peace.

And it shall be, when the Lord your God gives you rest from all your enemies round about you, in the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession to inherit, that you shall blot out the name of Amalek from under heaven. You shall not forget.
Judas withdrew from the citadel and encamped at Beth-zechariah opposite the king’s camp.
The king rose early in the morning and set his army moving rapidly along the road to Beth-zechariah. The forces prepared for battle and sounded the trumpets.
They showed the elephants the blood of grapes and mulberries to ready them for battle.

They divided the beasts among the phalanxes. Beside each elephant they stationed a thousand men armoured in chain mail, with bronze helmets on their heads, and five hundred picked cavalry were assigned to each beast.
They were in position beforehand wherever the beast was; wherever it went, they went together and did not leave it.
Strong, covered wooden towers were on them, secured by devices upon each beast. On each were four fighting men and its Indian driver.
He stationed the remaining cavalry on either side, on the two wings of the army, threatening the enemy and shielding the phalanxes.
One part of the king’s army spread out on the high mountains and others on the low ground. They advanced securely and in order.
Everyone who heard the sound of their multitude, the march of the multitude, and the clash of weapons was shaken, for the army was exceedingly large and strong.

Look, upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace! Celebrate your feasts, Judah; repay your vows. For they will no longer pass through you into decay. It has been completed; it has been removed.
One who breathes into your face has come up, rescuing from affliction. Watch the road; hold your waist firm; act courageously with great strength,
because the Lord turned away Jacob’s arrogance, as Israel’s arrogance; for those shaking them out shook out both them and their vine branches; they ruined
the weapons of their might from among people, mighty men playing in fire. The reins of their chariots are on the day of his preparation, and the horsemen will be thrown into uproar
Their nobles will remember and flee by day; they will weaken on their journey, hurry to the walls and prepare their defenses.
